section.title: Increasing and decreasing functions
section.p: A speedometer does not only tell how fast a car is moving. Its sign tells the direction of motion. Positive velocity means position is increasing. Negative velocity means position is decreasing.
The same idea works for any differentiable function.

exercise.title: Why does the sign of f' control increase and decrease?

statement.p: If f'(x)>0 on an interval, f is increasing there. In your own words, why is that a statement about rates rather than a statement about the values of f being positive?

hint.p: f' measures how f is changing, not how large f is. A negative function can still be increasing.

exercise.title: Why must we name the interval when we say a function is increasing?

statement.p: A function can increase on one interval and decrease on another. In your own words, why is increasing a claim about pairs of inputs on a chosen interval, not a label that a function either has or fails to have forever?

hint.p: The definition compares f(x_1) and f(x_2) only for inputs inside the interval under discussion.

subsection.title: The first derivative sign rule
subsection.p: The examples point to the rule we want.

note.title: First derivative sign rule
note.p: Suppose f is continuous on an interval I and differentiable at the interior points of I.
throughout the interior of I, then f is increasing on I.

subsection.p: This rule is one of the most useful tools in differential calculus. Its proof will come from the Mean Value Theorem in Section . For now, the meaning is visible from local linear approximation:
When h>0, moving to the right by a small amount, a positive f'(x) gives a positive change in f. A negative f'(x) gives a negative change in f.
The Mean Value Theorem will explain why this local information controls the whole interval.

subsection.p: The derivative does not need to be drawn. The sign chart may contain all the information we need.

exercise.title: What information does a first-derivative sign chart actually record?

statement.p: A sign chart splits the line at the places where f' is zero or undefined, then records the sign of f' on each piece. In your own words, why do those split points belong on the chart, and what graph information is the chart trying to make visible without drawing the graph?

hint.p: The sign of f' can change only where f' is zero or fails to exist. Between those points, the chart is a dictionary from rate to rising or falling.

exercise.title: Why is a critical number a candidate rather than a conclusion?

statement.p: A number c in the domain of f is critical if f'(c)=0 or if f'(c) does not exist. In your own words, why does that make c worth inspecting, and why does it not yet promise a high point or a low point?

hint.p: Think of x^3 at 0, or of |x| at 0. One is critical and does not turn around; the other is critical because of a corner.
